situation.text: Hoje você conhece Jonah, de Denver. Abastecer e pagar no posto.

pages.goal: Hoje você aprende a falar de transportes com o verbo take: take a bus, take a train, take a taxi.

pages.hook: On an American road trip, the gas station is a small stop with fuel, snacks and a restroom. You pick a pump, choose a grade and pay by the gallon.
pages.polite: Say **“Pump number three, please”** if you pay inside. Many people simply pay at the pump with a card.

mythfact.s: In the USA gas is sold by the gallon.
mythfact.why: Prices on the big sign are per gallon, not per liter.

mythfact.s: Most gas stations in the USA have a free attendant who pumps for you.
mythfact.why: Most people pump their own gas. New Jersey is a well-known exception, and Oregon has allowed self-service only recently.

mythfact.s: Regular and premium are two kinds of gasoline.
mythfact.why: Premium has a higher octane number and costs more.

mythfact.s: A gas station only sells gas.
mythfact.why: Many also sell water, snacks and coffee, and have a restroom.

compare.br: In Brazil an attendant, the frentista, usually fills the tank, and many cars can use ethanol or gasoline.
compare.us: In the USA most drivers fill the car themselves and pay by the gallon.
compare.tip: Choose regular unless your car manual says premium.

pages.title: Cultural spotlight
Reading quest — A stop in Denver
text: We were on a long road trip from Denver to Utah. After two hours, the fuel light came on. “We are running on empty!” my friend Jonah said. We stopped at a gas station near the highway.

The station had six pumps. We parked at pump number three. Jonah went inside and said to the clerk, “**Hi! Pump number three, please.**” The clerk asked, “**How much gas do you want?**” “**Twenty dollars, please**,” Jonah answered.

“**Do you want regular or premium?**” the clerk asked. “**Regular, please**,” Jonah said. “**Do you need anything else?**” “**A bottle of water**,” Jonah said. The clerk said, “**That’s twenty-two dollars**.” Jonah paid with a card.
I filled the tank. First, I lifted the nozzle. Then I put it in the car and pressed the handle. The numbers on the pump went up fast. Finally, I hung the nozzle back and closed the cap.
We used the restroom, and I bought a coffee. The clerk smiled and said, “**Drive safe!**” “**Thanks!**” I said. The sun was low, and the mountains looked red and gold.
Back on the road, Jonah drank his water and I watched the map. A small stop like this one is a good moment to rest and check the car.
